title: The minor pentatonic scale
summary: The five-note scale behind most rock and blues solos.

steps.title: Five notes, infinite licks
steps.body: The minor pentatonic uses only 5 notes per octave: 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. By dropping the 2nd and b6 from natural minor, you remove most of the half-step tension and end up with a scale that 'just works' over minor and dominant chords. Almost every rock and blues solo is built from it.

steps.title: A minor pentatonic, position 1
steps.body: The most-played shape in guitar history. Roots are in orange.

steps.title: Run the scale up and down
Why it works over Am AND A7
steps.body: Over Am the chord tones are A C E. The pentatonic supplies all of them, plus D and G as 'tension' tones that resolve naturally. Over A7 (A C# E G) the b3 (C) clashes with C#... and that clash is the blues. The pentatonic intentionally leans into that friction -- which is why bending the b3 up toward the major 3rd is one of the most-used moves on the instrument.
